about: The guided tour script. One source: tour/index.html renders it, and the home page chat (index.html) reads its chat block. Links are relative to the site root; links starting with # point inside the tour page. {name} is the name the visitor picks for the bot and {you} is what the bot calls the visitor. Every capability claim must be true today; plans carry a 'coming' status. Bot windows are scripted replays, never real logs. Bills and shopping are pretend.

start.unknown: Ha, I'd love to chat freely, but on this page I'm a script, not a live bot. Type tour to start again, or pick a button.

chat.hello: Hey out there! I'm EA-bot, a small helper bot with a big notebook. No typing needed: pick one of three, or save one for later.

nodes.title: EA-bot
nodes.fact: First surprise: I'm not the model. I'm the harness around it: the rules, tools, checks and notes that make a model useful.

nodes.title: Jobs side by side
nodes.chip: How do you get work done?
nodes.fact: Give me ten to-dos at once and I split them into jobs and run them side by side. Ten workers at once has been done on the owner's machine.

nodes.title: A copy each
nodes.chip: Why don't workers collide?
nodes.fact: Each worker gets its own git worktree: a separate copy of the code. A worker cannot break the main copy, and nobody trips over anybody.

nodes.title: One brief, one task
nodes.chip: What does a worker get?
nodes.fact: Every job becomes a written brief with one task and a check for done. The board has six phases, and a task leaves a phase only when that phase's exit check is true.

nodes.title: Not tied to one model
nodes.chip: Which AI model are you?
nodes.fact: More than one. A short rules file, called the map, is linked into Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI and backpass. Change it once and all five see it next session.

see.label: How it works: one rules file

nodes.title: It runs today
nodes.chip: Is this real or a design?
nodes.fact: It runs, in daily use on the owner's machine. One of my workers built these pages. On one day four workers ran in parallel, and three delivered a reviewed pull request.

nodes.title: Scripts, not guesses
nodes.chip: How do you stay fast?
nodes.fact: Work that must go the same way every time moves out of the model and into scripts: hooks, checks and builders. They are faster, cheaper and never guess.

nodes.title: Checked three times
nodes.chip: How do I know it's right?
nodes.fact: Nothing lands until it is checked three times. The worker backs each claim with a command or a file read, the gates check again, and then you decide.

nodes.title: Hooks
nodes.chip: What stops a bad command?
nodes.fact: Hooks: scripts the tool must run before an action. One blocks file writes through the shell and says to use the editor tools. It has blocked commands in a scout's own session.

nodes.title: You hold the big buttons
nodes.chip: Who presses the big buttons?
nodes.fact: You do. Only you merge, push to the main branch, delete, publish, send or spend. I stop at a draft and ask.

nodes.title: Honest gaps
nodes.chip: Any weak spots?
nodes.fact: Yes, and they stay on the site. A manual once said workers run with permission checks on. A check counted: all 10 running workers had them off. The manual was fixed. A safer mode is a one-line switch, not switched on yet.

see.label: Harness flow: checks that proved it wrong

nodes.title: Pages, not a terminal
nodes.chip: How do you show your work?
nodes.fact: Every report, plan or draft for you becomes a page you can mark up. Your notes go back to the agent that wrote it, which fixes the page and asks again.

nodes.title: Memory in files
nodes.chip: Do you remember me?
nodes.fact: Not in my head. In files: the rules, the chat, a store of reports and notes, and an index that says where things are.

nodes.title: The work index
nodes.chip: How do you find old work?
nodes.fact: A script rebuilds an index of every work folder at the start of each session: no model, no network. It exists because an agent once searched the web for work that was already on disk.

nodes.title: Skills as recipe cards
nodes.chip: How do you learn new tricks?
nodes.fact: Skills are recipe cards. I see a one-line description of each, and load the full card only when a task needs it.

nodes.title: Rules that improve
nodes.chip: Do you get better over time?
nodes.fact: A tool called backpass reads my old sessions and proposes edits to my own rules. It never writes them. You approve each one.
nodes.status: nightly job installed, not yet seen to run

nodes.title: The second brain
nodes.chip: Where does what we learn go?
nodes.fact: Into a second brain. A note lands in an inbox the same day, is boiled down to one idea, then linked to its neighbours. No note is born alone.

nodes.title: Three talk modes
nodes.chip: Can you talk my way?
nodes.fact: I can talk in three modes. ADHD mode puts the key point first. Caveman mode is very short. STE100 mode uses Simplified Technical English.

nodes.title: The charter
nodes.chip: What's our deal?
nodes.fact: A chatbot sets no contract. We do. We both organize life and build knowledge. The third task matters most: teach it to each other, and check the other has learned it.

nodes.title: Teach it back
nodes.chip: How do you check I learned it?
nodes.fact: At the end of a tour track I ask you to teach it back in your own words. A teach-back shows the gaps a re-read hides.

nodes.title: Agents as vendors
nodes.chip: How should I think about you?
nodes.fact: Like a contract with vendors. You scope the work, write down who may do what, ask for status, and accept work only on evidence.

persona.ask_name: First things first. I don't have a name yet. What should I be called?
persona.named: {name}. I like it. Fits me like a fresh coat of paint.
persona.ask_you: And what should I call you?
persona.friday: A good way to think about me: like a Man Friday, a Chotu or a Jeeves. The trusted helper you call to solve any problem.

lines.text: This is EA-bot, and you can call me {name}. I'm a smart harness agent built on top of an LLM. I'm not the model itself. I'm the harness around it: the rules, tools, checks and notes that make a model useful.
I'm not tied to one model. The same rules load into Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Gemini CLI, so I can work across them.
Give me ten to-dos at once and I'll split them into jobs and run them side by side. Ten workers at once has been done on the owner's machine.
I double-check. Each worker backs every claim with a command or a file it read, and the gates check again before you see it.
Missing a skill? I'll go find it and install it through a set workflow, and you approve it first.
It's a bit like magic, except every trick is written down. Anything marked coming is a plan, not a feature yet.

intro.links_label: Before we go on, the small print:
intro.charter_lead: Now our deal. I call it the charter.

charter.title: The charter
lines: Whenever you use a chatbot, you are not setting a contract. Here we are.
The human and the AI both have two tasks:
tasks: Build knowledge about the world at large.
charter.third: And the third, most critical: teach this to each other, and make sure the other has learned it.

Write one idea in each note.

trust.title: Capability, security and performance
trust.lead: The small print, in plain words. It describes the owner's own setup today.

sections.title: Capability: what I can do, and how I learn new tricks

points.text: I work in a terminal and an agent window manager, with full automation access on the owner's machine. I can run commands, edit files and start other agents.
I split work into jobs and run them side by side. Ten workers at once has been done.
My rules load into Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and Gemini CLI, so I am not tied to one model.
Skills are recipe cards. I see a one-line description of each, and load the full card only when a task needs it.
When a skill is missing, I find it and install it through a set workflow, with your approval.

sections.title: Security: what I can touch, who approves, and secrets

points.text: Each worker gets its own copy of the code (a git worktree), so a worker cannot break the main copy.
Every worker runs in its own window that you can open and watch, and its tool calls are logged.
Control mode today: workers skip permission checks by default. That is the standing setting, and the owner knows it.
A safer, model-reviewed permission mode is a one-line switch. It is not switched on yet.
You hold the big buttons. Only you merge, push to the main branch, delete, publish, send or spend. I stop and ask.
Secrets never go in files, commits, logs or prompts. That rule is in the rules file every agent reads at the start.
A hook blocks commands that would print a secret, and another warns on text shaped like a key.
points.status: installed, not yet proven in a test

daily.label: Daily safety check
daily.line: Once a day, send me this:
daily.prompt: Safety check: what did you change since yesterday, what is waiting for my OK, and did any secret touch a file?

sections.title: Performance: speed and reliability from scripts

points.text: Work that must go the same way every time moves out of the model and into deterministic harness scripts: hooks, checks and builders. They are faster, cheaper and never guess.
Example: the work index is rebuilt by a script at the start of each session. No model, no network.
More harness research is on the way.

paths.title: Help you organize
paths.summary: Hand me the whole to-do pile. I sort it, run it side by side, and check it.
paths.intro: Let's get you organized, {you}. Three steps.
paths.use_prompt: Here is everything on my plate. Sort it into jobs: start now, needs me, can wait. Run the ones that can run in parallel, check each result, and stop before anything that sends, pays, merges or deletes: <your list>

steps.title: Dump the list
steps.plain: Tell me everything on your plate. Messy is fine. I sort it into jobs: what I can start now, what needs you, what can wait.
steps.tech: Each job becomes a written brief with one task and a check for done. The board has six phases, and a task leaves a phase only when that phase's exit check is true.
steps.prompt: Here is everything on my plate. Sort it into jobs: start now, needs me, can wait. Give each job one line saying what done looks like: <your list>

steps.title: Run them side by side
steps.plain: I hand the jobs to workers and run them at once. Each worker has its own copy of the work, so nobody trips over anybody.
steps.tech: One git worktree and one brief per worker. Workers report status lines back to me. Each claim is backed by a command or a file read.
steps.prompt: Run these jobs in parallel where they do not depend on each other. Tell me which ones must wait for another, and why: <jobs>

steps.title: Check, then you decide
steps.plain: When work comes back, I check it, the gates check it, and then it's your call. I never merge, send or pay on my own.
steps.tech: Hooks block unsafe commands before they run. Only the owner holds merge, publish, send and spend.
steps.prompt: Before you show me any result, tell me how you checked it. Then stop and wait for my OK on anything that sends, pays, merges or deletes.

paths.teach_back: Explain back to me how my to-do list turns into checked work, and which steps need my yes. Then ask me one question to check I understood.

paths.title: Manage your knowledge (and keep mine up to date)
paths.summary: What we learn goes into a second brain, sorted and linked. My own rules get updated too, with your approval.
paths.intro: Knowledge time, {you}. Yours first, then mine.
paths.use_prompt: At the end of this chat, write a short note on what we decided and learned. Find the closest notes I already have, then tell me whether to merge, link or keep it separate. File nothing until I approve.

steps.title: Catch it the same day
steps.plain: At the end of a session I write a short note: what we decided, what we learned, what is still open. It goes to an inbox first, not straight into the brain.
steps.tech: Session notes are dated files in an inbox folder. Raw capture is not knowledge yet; it waits for the sort step.
steps.prompt: Write a capture note for this chat: goals, decisions, what we learned, open questions. Under 150 words. Do not file it yet.

steps.title: Sort it and link it
steps.plain: Each note is boiled down to one idea and checked against what is already there: merge it, link it, or make a new note. No note is born alone.
steps.tech: An index lists every note and is rebuilt at the start of a session. Search local notes first, then the web.
steps.prompt: Here is a new note. Find the closest notes I already have. Tell me: merge into one, link to it, or keep it separate, and why: <note>

steps.title: Keep mine up to date too
steps.plain: I learn as well. At night, a tool reads my old sessions and proposes changes to my own rules. It never writes them. You approve each one.
steps.tech: backpass reads tool logs and proposes rule edits backed by quotes from two or more sessions. The nightly job is installed but has not yet been seen to run.
steps.status: installed, not yet seen to run
steps.prompt: Look back at our chats this week. List each time I corrected you. For each, say whether the fix belongs in your rules, a skill, or nowhere, and write the exact wording. Change nothing until I approve.

paths.teach_back: Explain back to me how a new topic reaches my second brain, and how your own rules get updated. Then ask me one question to check I understood.

paths.title: Use ours
paths.summary: An opinionated way to store notes and cross-reference them. Three tracks.
paths.intro: Use our method, {you}. Fair warning: it's opinionated. One idea per note, every note linked to its neighbours, and nothing filed without a review. Pick a track.
paths.use_prompt: From now on, keep my notes this way: one idea per note, a one-line description on each, and a link from every new note to at least one existing note. Nothing is filed until I approve it. Start with this: <what is on your mind>

tracks.title: How First Mate works
tracks.summary: Six parts of an agent harness, in four steps.
tracks.use_prompt: Explain how you work in six parts: pipeline, roles, memory, skills, tools and safety. One line each. Mark anything that is designed but not proven.

steps.title: Pipeline and roles
steps.plain: You ask once. First Mate splits the ask into small jobs and hands each one to a worker. Scouts find facts. Builders change code. You decide at the start and at the end.
steps.tech: One orchestrator session writes a brief per task and starts each worker in its own git worktree. Each role has written permissions: a scout reports, a builder opens a pull request, and only the owner merges.
steps.prompt: Split this goal into small jobs. For each job, say who should do it (a scout to find facts, or a builder to make a change) and what proof of done looks like: <your goal>

steps.title: Memory and skills
steps.plain: The agent does not remember in its head. It writes things down: rules, reports, session notes, and an index of where things are. Skills are recipe cards it opens only when a task needs one.
steps.tech: Four kinds of memory: rules (always loaded), the chat (squeezed into a summary at compaction), the work store (reports, briefs, notes) and a generated index rebuilt at session start. Skills load by progressive disclosure: a one-line description is always visible, the full text loads on demand.
steps.prompt: Before you answer, list what you already know about this topic from our earlier notes, and say where each fact came from. If there are no notes, say so: <topic>

steps.title: Tools and safety
steps.plain: Workers use tools: a browser, GitHub, a terminal. Safety means drafts, not sends. Nothing is merged, published, sent or paid until you say yes.
steps.tech: Hooks run before tool calls and block unsafe actions. Each worker has an isolated copy of the code. A gate checks work before push. The owner alone holds merge, publish, send and spend.
steps.prompt: For this task, list every step that is hard to undo (send, pay, delete, publish). Stop before each one and ask me: <task>

steps.title: See it in action
steps.plain: Here a scout and a helper do one pretend job. Click a window to step through what each one thinks and does.
steps.tech: A replay is a scripted sample written for this page. It shows the shape of a run: a brief, evidence, a draft, and a stop for approval.
steps.prompt: Show your work as short numbered steps: what you checked, what you found, what you will do next, and where you will stop for my OK.

tracks.teach_back: In your own words, how does a job move from my ask to done? Name the six parts as you go. Then ask me one question to check I understood.

tracks.title: The second brain
tracks.summary: How a new topic gets in, gets sorted, and stays useful.
tracks.use_prompt: Run the intake checklist on this topic: capture, distill, connect, retrieve, review. Show me the result of each step before you file anything: <topic>

steps.title: Capture: how soon a topic gets in
steps.plain: A new topic gets in the same day. At the end of a session, the agent writes a short note: what was decided, what was learned, what is still open. It lands in an inbox, not straight in the brain.
steps.tech: Session summaries are dated files in an inbox folder. Nothing in the inbox counts as knowledge yet. It is raw capture, waiting for the distill step.
steps.prompt: Write a capture note for this chat: goals, decisions, what we learned, open questions. Under 150 words. Do not file it yet.

steps.title: Distill and connect: sorting against what is there
steps.plain: Each capture is boiled down to one idea per note. Before a new note is made, the agent looks for a note on the same idea. If one exists, the new point is merged in. If not, a new note is made and linked to its neighbours.
steps.tech: Atomic notes, each with a one-line description. Search the index for overlap first, then merge, link or create. Every new note links to at least one existing note, and the index gets one row.
steps.prompt: Here is a new note. Find the closest notes I already have. Tell me: merge into one, link to it, or keep it separate, and why: <note>

steps.title: Retrieve and review
steps.plain: When a task starts, the agent reads the index first and opens only the notes it needs. On a set rhythm, a review asks of each note: still true? still used? Notes are updated, merged or retired.
steps.tech: Retrieval is index first, local files before the web. Review looks for decay: stale dates, notes with no links in or out, duplicates. Nothing reaches the curated notes until a human approves it.
steps.prompt: Review these notes for decay. For each one say keep, update, merge or retire, with one reason: <notes>

steps.title: The intake-and-review checklist
steps.plain: Use this list each time a new topic comes up. Tick each step before you move on.
steps.tech: The same five-step loop runs for every source: a chat, a lesson, an article. The order matters: connect before you file, so no note is born alone.

checklist.name: Capture
checklist.text: Write the raw note the same day. Inbox only.

checklist.name: Distill
checklist.text: One idea per note, with a one-line description.

checklist.name: Connect
checklist.text: Find the nearest notes. Merge, link or create. Add an index row.

checklist.name: Retrieve
checklist.text: Start each task from the index, local notes before the web.

checklist.name: Review
checklist.text: On a rhythm: keep, update, merge or retire. A human approves.

steps.prompt: Run the intake checklist on this topic: capture, distill, connect, retrieve, review. Show me the result of each step: <topic>

tracks.teach_back: Explain back to me how a new topic enters my second brain and how it is checked against the notes I already have. Then point out one step I skipped.

tracks.title: The life organizer
tracks.summary: Pretend bills and shopping, run by small bots.
tracks.use_prompt: Here are my bills and shopping needs for this week. Split them into small jobs, one per helper, and give each job a stop rule: report or draft, never pay or order. <your list>

steps.title: One ask, small bots
steps.plain: You say: sort out this week's bills and shopping. First Mate splits it. A scout reads the bills. A helper drafts the shopping order. Each bot does one small job.
steps.tech: The orchestrator writes two briefs. Each bot gets only what it needs and a stop rule: report or draft, never pay.
steps.prompt: Here are my bills and shopping needs for the week. Split them into small jobs, one per helper, and give each job a stop rule: <your list>

steps.title: Watch the bots
steps.plain: Click a window to see each bot think, one step at a time. The bills, the shop and the money are all pretend.
steps.tech: Scripted replay, not a live log. Note the helper reads the scout's report before it adds up the week. Bots share results through reports, not chat.
steps.prompt: Show your work as short numbered steps: what you checked, what you found, what you will do next, and where you will stop for my OK.

steps.title: You give the word
steps.plain: The bots come back with drafts: a bill ready to pay and a cart ready to order. Nothing is paid or ordered until you say yes.
steps.tech: Spend is an owner-only action. The helper stops at a draft. Approval is a separate, explicit step that the bot cannot take.
steps.prompt: Draft the payment and the order, but do not send either. Show me one line for each and wait for my yes.

tracks.teach_back: Tell me which steps in this week's chores you may do on your own, and which ones need my yes. Then ask me one question to check we agree.

paths.title: Build your own second brain
paths.summary: Start from scratch with plain files. Three steps.
paths.intro: Build your own, from scratch. Plain text files are enough. Here are three steps.
paths.use_prompt: Help me set up a second brain in plain markdown files: an inbox, a notes folder and an index. Give me the folder layout and a template for one note.

steps.title: Start with three parts
steps.plain: Make one folder with three parts: an inbox for raw notes, a notes folder for finished ideas, and one index page that lists them.
steps.tech: inbox/, notes/ and INDEX.md. Plain markdown, one idea per file, a short kebab-case file name. The index has one line per note: a link and a one-line hook.
steps.prompt: Help me set up a second brain in plain markdown files: an inbox, a notes folder and an index. Give me the folder layout and a template for one note.

steps.title: Write your first linked notes
steps.plain: Take one thing you learned this week. Write it as one short note. Then write a second note and link the two.
steps.tech: Each note has a title, a one-line description, the idea, and links written as [[note-name]]. A link to a note that does not exist yet is fine. It marks a note worth writing.
steps.prompt: Turn this into one note: a title, a one-line description, the idea in under 100 words, and two [[links]] to notes I should write next: <what I learned>

steps.title: Set a review rhythm
steps.plain: Once a week, empty the inbox and look at a few old notes. Keep, update, merge or retire each one.
steps.tech: Inbox to zero: each item becomes a note, a merge, or is dropped. Then sample older notes for decay.
steps.prompt: It is review day. Go through my inbox one item at a time: make it a note, merge it into one I have, or drop it. Ask me only when unsure.

paths.teach_back: Explain back to me the three parts of my second brain and what happens on review day. Then ask me one question to check I understood.

paths.title: Learn deeply
paths.summary: The LearnHarness route: guided lessons with teach-back. Three steps.
paths.intro: Learn one hard topic deeply. This route uses LearnHarness, an open-source app where AI agents teach a topic and build a knowledge graph as you go.
paths.use_prompt: I want to learn <topic> deeply. Ask me three questions to find what I already know, then propose a plan of five short lessons.

steps.title: Pick one hard topic
steps.plain: Choose one topic you want to really know. The teacher first asks what you know, then plans short lessons.
steps.tech: LearnHarness describes itself as an agent harness for learning difficult things. It is open source (AGPL-3.0) and runs on your own machine.
steps.prompt: I want to learn <topic> deeply. Ask me three questions to find what I already know, then propose a plan of five short lessons.

steps.title: Learn by teaching back
steps.plain: After each lesson, explain it back in your own words. The teacher checks your answer and points to the gaps.
steps.tech: This is the charter's third task: make sure the other has learned it. A teach-back shows the gaps a re-read hides.
steps.prompt: Here is my explanation of <concept>. Grade it: what is right, what is missing, what is wrong. Then ask me one question about the gap.

steps.title: File what you learned
steps.plain: Each lesson ends with one note in your second brain, linked to what you already know.
steps.tech: The lesson note goes through the same intake checklist as any other topic: capture, distill, connect, retrieve, review.
steps.prompt: Write one note from today's lesson: the idea, one example, and links to two notes I already have.

paths.teach_back: Pick the hardest idea from this lesson and ask me to teach it back to you. Grade my answer and tell me what to review.

weekly-chores.title: Replay: this week's bills and shopping
weekly-chores.note: A scripted sample, not a live log. The bills, the shop and the money are pretend.

windows.name: Scout · bills
windows.brief: Read this week's bills. Report what is due. Pay nothing.

steps.think: The brief says read and report. Paying is not my job. First, find the bills.
steps.do: Opened the pretend bills folder. Three bills.

steps.think: Which are due this week? Water is due Friday. Phone and power are due later in the month.
Is that amount normal? Last month was 39.80. Up about 6 percent. Small, but worth one line.

steps.say: One bill due this week: water, 42.10 by Friday, about 6% up on last month. Two bills due later. Nothing paid.

windows.end: Report filed. Stopped: paying needs the owner.

windows.name: Helper · shopping
windows.brief: Draft this week's shopping order from the pantry list. Order nothing.

steps.think: Draft only. First, what is running low?
steps.do: Read the pretend pantry list: coffee, rice and soap are low.

steps.think: Price them at the pretend shop: 9 + 6 + 4.
The weekly budget note says 60 for bills and shopping. The scout's report says water is 42.10. 19 + 42.10 = 61.10, so 1.10 over. Flag it. Do not decide for the owner.
steps.do: Read the scout's report and the budget note.

steps.say: Draft cart ready: coffee, rice, soap, 19. With the water bill the week is 61.10, 1.10 over the budget of 60. Option: drop the soap. Nothing ordered.

windows.end: Draft ready. Waiting for your OK.

weekly-chores.after: Both bots stopped at a draft. You decide what is paid and ordered.

end.track_done: Nice work, {you}. That's the track. Now the charter's favourite part: teach it back. Send me this and I'll check we both got it.
end.more: Pick another path, or type tour to start over. I don't get tired.
